steps.title: Check normality first
steps.answers: How do you check that data are normal enough for a t test?
steps.opens: What if the data are ranks or not normal?
steps.statement: Before a Z or t test, look at hist() and run shapiro.test(): p > 0.05 means normal enough; a small p means use the rank tests instead.

explain.text: shapiro.test() asks whether the data could come from a normal distribution. Its p-value works the other way round from most tests: a small p (≤ 0.05) is evidence against normality. The histogram shows why: skew, two peaks or outliers. With large samples tiny departures become significant, so the picture matters as much as the p.

figure.caption: The shape a t test assumes: one symmetric peak.

lines.explain: H₀: the data are normal; p > 0.05 → normal enough

code.interpret: If Shapiro rejects normality, go to the weakly measured branch (wilcox.test).

steps.intuition: Check that the key fits the lock before you turn it.
steps.misconception: A significant Shapiro test is a good result.

misconceptionFigure.caption: Read it the other way round.

check.q: shapiro.test() gives p = 0.002. Which test do you use for two independent groups?
check.a: Mann–Whitney U, wilcox.test(y ~ group): the data are not normal.
